objects.title: Stereoscope and stereograph
objects.date_range: 1838 onward; popular handheld Holmes design from 1861; object-specific scanned example 1905-1920

inventors.name: Charles Wheatstone
inventors.role: published an early binocular stereoscope in 1838

inventors.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes
inventors.role: described a practical handheld viewer in 1861

objects.manufacturer: A. Mattey (French maker, founded 1872), for the Smithsonian 3D object 2017.111.16 only
objects.original_purpose: View paired images as an apparently three-dimensional scene, including photographs of distant places and events.
objects.mechanism: Two slightly different views are presented separately to the eyes through lenses; binocular fusion produces perceived depth.
objects.historical_significance: Stereographs became mass visual entertainment and domestic access to distant scenes; the underlying binocular principle persists in 3D imaging.
objects.technology_afterlife: Evolved through different viewer and image formats; not a failed invention.

objects.title: Zoetrope (commercial cylindrical form)
objects.date_range: Horner's Daedaleum described 1833/1834; commercial zoetrope from the 1860s

inventors.name: William Ensign Lincoln
inventors.role: associated with the later US commercial patent/form, assigned to Milton Bradley

objects.manufacturer: Milton Bradley & Company for catalogued Smithsonian examples
objects.original_purpose: Optical entertainment and demonstration of apparent motion.
objects.mechanism: Sequential drawings arranged inside a rotating slotted drum are seen in brief successive glimpses through the slits, creating apparent motion.
objects.historical_significance: Popular optical toy and important precursor in animation history.
objects.technology_afterlife: Commercially popular as a toy; later adopted in art and education. The frame-and-view principle remains useful in explaining animation.

objects.title: Edison's tinfoil phonograph
objects.manufacturer: John Kruesi, machinist, built the first working machine from Edison's sketch
objects.original_purpose: Developed from attempts to record/repeat telegraph signals and consider recording telephone speech; demonstrated as a novelty, with proposed dictation, music, teaching, and preservation uses.
objects.mechanism: A hand-cranked tinfoil-wrapped cylinder moves beneath a diaphragm and stylus. Sound vibrations emboss a vertical hill-and-dale groove; playback stylus follows it and vibrates the diaphragm.
objects.historical_significance: Established a working demonstration of sound recording and playback; drew immediate public attention.
objects.technology_afterlife: Fragile foil and difficult operation limited repeated use. Wax-cylinder refinements superseded the tinfoil form; sound recording continued and expanded.

objects.title: Pneumatic postal tube system (city-specific networks)
objects.date_range: London postal tubes from 1863; Philadelphia US service from 1893; New York 1897-1953, interrupted 1918-1922

inventors.name: Birney Clark Batcheller
inventors.role: engineer and patent holder associated with principal American postal tube process

objects.manufacturer: Private contractors including Tubular Dispatch Company in early New York service; network operators and contractors varied by city
objects.original_purpose: Move letters and small parcels rapidly between urban post offices, railway stations, and exchange points, avoiding congested streets.
objects.mechanism: A sealed canister carrying mail travels through a tube using pressure or vacuum from station machinery; routing stations direct carriers to destination points.
objects.historical_significance: A genuinely used and high-volume urban mail transport infrastructure. New York's system grew to about 27 miles and carried millions of letters.
objects.technology_afterlife: US mail systems closed amid high operating costs, fixed infrastructure, and changing transport economics; New York service ended Dec. 31, 1953. Pneumatic conveyance continues in other modern settings.
